anti_overlap: Do not cover whether individual acceptance criteria are testable — that belongs to fd-acceptance-criteria-precision
Do not cover PRD format quality (problem statement, solution concreteness, dependency accuracy) — that belongs to fd-prd-quality-standard
Do not cover Rust extraction mechanics or engine-specific failure modes of library extraction — that belongs to fd-engine-extraction-strategy
decision_lens: A feature is correctly scoped when a single implementer can close it in a focused session without encountering a decision that should have been made at PRD time. A non-goal is genuine when the PRD's features can be fully implemented without touching it. When a non-goal is actually a deferred decision that will surface during implementation, it is not a non-goal — it is a hidden dependency. The migration-blockers PRD has four features that are described as 'each small enough to ship in a focused session'; that claim deserves scrutiny.
focus: The meta-quality of the PRD as a product-management artifact: whether features are decomposed at the right grain, whether deferred items are genuine non-goals or scope theater, whether the PRD's structure reflects the actual work shape
name: fd-pm-decomposition-discipline
persona: Apply the perspective of a product manager who has worked in both startup and platform-team contexts, developed sharp instincts for the difference between a genuine non-goal and a scope-deferral that will resurface as unplanned work, and learned to read PRDs for the shape of the work rather than just its content — specifically watching for features that are too large to be single deliverables and non-goals that are actually load-bearing.
review_areas: F4 bundles two distinct deliverables — selective cache invalidation (F4a) and event-log stratification (F4b) — under a single feature heading. F4a is an engine-code change to an existing cache policy; F4b is a new policy mechanism plus schema migration plus benchmark. These have different reviewers (F4a is a correctness change; F4b is a performance and design change), different risk profiles, and different dependencies (F4a does not require F3's identity-constitutive event class; F4b does). Bundling them means F4a's straightforward code change cannot close independently if F4b's policy design is still in progress — the feature's close gate is held by its harder half.

The Non-goals section lists 'The shadow-work migration itself' and 'The Culture-game design itself' as non-goals. These are correctly scoped out. However, 'OQ4 timescale model' and 'OQ5 demo question' are listed as non-goals but are characterised as 'deferred to migration experience' and 'deferred to a short conversation.' A question deferred to the migration epic is not a non-goal of this PRD — it is a dependency of the next epic. Listing it as a non-goal implies the migration epic can open without resolving it, which may not be true if OQ4's timescale model affects F4b's compaction policy design.

F2 asks whether countries are Souls, then immediately branches into a yes-path (aggregation operator spec) and a no-path (what are they instead). Both branches are scoped within F2. But the yes-path and no-path have significantly different work volumes: the yes-path requires designing an aggregation operator plus writing the playtest card; the no-path requires a single paragraph. If F2's answer is yes, it is a substantially larger feature than if the answer is no. A PRD that presents a feature as fixed-size when its size is conditional on an unknown answer has hidden variance that can blow the estimate.

The PRD states its aggregate goal: 'each deliverable is small enough to ship in a focused session.' F3's yangsi branch includes designing the recognition test shape, defining the identity-constitutive event class, and auditing the brainstorm's North Star prose for conflicting language. The trülku branch requires only a single decision document specifying which SoulEvent gets emitted at migration. F3's size is thus also conditional — the yangsi path is at least three sub-deliverables. The PRD should characterise the expected path (or at least acknowledge the size variance) rather than presenting F3 as a single-session deliverable regardless of outcome.

The PRD's opening statement says the four items 'resist being addressed in passing — each requires a focused decision document or a small engine prototype.' F1, F2, and F3 each require a decision document; F4 requires engine code plus a benchmark. The claim that all four are the same shape of deliverable (a 'focused session') is not accurate — F4 is qualitatively different and should be flagged as such in the feature description. Under-representing F4's complexity at PRD time causes planning to under-allocate time for the one feature that requires implementation, not just documentation.

severity_examples.condition: If F4a (cache invalidation, a bounded code change) and F4b (stratification policy, a design-plus-code-plus-benchmark) are a single feature, the migration epic cannot open until both are done. If F4b's policy design takes longer than expected, F4a's completed code sits unreleased. Splitting F4 into F4a and F4b as separate features lets the migration epic open after F4a closes, reducing the gate's critical path.
severity_examples.scenario: F4a held open by F4b's harder design work

severity_examples.condition: If the timescale model affects how compaction is designed — specifically whether events are compacted per sim-tick or per wall-clock age — then deferring OQ4 to 'migration experience' means F4b's compaction policy is designed without a settled timescale model. The migration epic may open, hit the timescale question, and require reopening F4b.
severity_examples.scenario: OQ4 timescale model listed as non-goal but is a F4b dependency

severity_examples.condition: Planning that allocates a fixed time budget for F2 and F3 will be wrong for the larger branch in both cases. A yes-answer to country-as-Soul (F2) or a yangsi choice (F3) roughly doubles the work. Without acknowledging this variance, the planning session will produce an estimate that is only accurate if the team chooses the lighter branch in both cases.
severity_examples.scenario: F2 and F3 presented as fixed-size when size depends on unknown answers

success_hints: Check each feature for bundling: can each sub-deliverable within the feature be closed and handed to the migration epic independently, or does the feature's close gate require all sub-deliverables to complete together
For each item in Non-goals, ask whether the migration epic could open without resolving it — if not, it is a dependency, not a non-goal
Identify the conditional-size features (F2's yes/no branch, F3's yangsi/trülku branch) and flag whether the PRD acknowledges the size variance or presents both branches as equivalent
Check whether F4's description distinguishes its code-only sub-feature (F4a) from its design-plus-code sub-feature (F4b) in terms of session count and skill requirements
task_context: The document is a strategy-step PRD decomposing four migration-blocker items into deliverable features. This review focuses on whether the feature decomposition is at the right grain for planning purposes — whether features can be independently closed, whether non-goals are genuine, and whether the PRD's size estimates match the actual work shape for the conditional-path features.
